reference.source: Auerbach's Wilderness Medicine / Bove and Davis' Diving Medicine
clinicalPearls: Occurs when a paranasal sinus cannot equalise pressure with the environment because its ostium is obstructed, classically during descent
The frontal and maxillary sinuses are most often affected, producing pain over the forehead, cheek, or around the eye
On descent the trapped sinus air is compressed relative to the surroundings, creating a squeeze that causes mucosal swelling, congestion, and bleeding into the sinus
Epistaxis or blood-tinged nasal discharge on ascent, when the injured mucosa is decompressed, is a common finding
Predisposing factors include upper respiratory infection, allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps, and other causes of ostial obstruction
Management is decongestion, avoiding diving or flying until the sinuses can equalise, and treating any underlying nasal pathology
Prevention centres on not diving or flying with nasal or sinus congestion and controlling rhinitis
reference.pathophysiology: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities that equalise pressure through their ostia into the nasal cavity. When an ostium is blocked by mucosal swelling, polyps, or secretions, the air within the sinus cannot equalise with rising ambient pressure on descent. The resulting relative negative pressure within the sinus draws fluid and blood from the mucosa into the cavity and causes mucosal engorgement and haemorrhage, producing pain and bleeding. On ascent, expanding trapped air or dislodged material can cause further discomfort and epistaxis.
additionalDifferentials: Facial pain from temporomandibular joint dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment correlating facial pain and epistaxis with the dive or flight profile
Anterior rhinoscopy or nasendoscopy to identify ostial obstruction, polyps, or inflammation
Otoscopy to assess for coexisting ear barotrauma
Sinus imaging (CT) in recurrent, severe, or diagnostically unclear cases
Assessment for underlying rhinitis or structural nasal abnormality
redFlags: Severe or persistent headache with neurological or visual symptoms
Features suggesting orbital or intracranial extension of infection
Recurrent barotrauma indicating significant untreated nasal or sinus disease
reference.prognosis: Sinus barotrauma usually settles within days to a couple of weeks with decongestion and avoidance of pressure changes; recurrence is likely if underlying nasal or sinus disease is not addressed, but serious complications are uncommon.
pitfalls: Continuing to dive or fly with nasal congestion and provoking recurrence
Failing to identify and treat underlying rhinitis, polyps, or structural obstruction
Missing secondary bacterial sinusitis after the injury
